The big story · A community experiment

The puts its own tools to the test

A two-week building challenge asks a simple question: can the ’s new tools help people make something useful?

A community-run building challenge opened on 2 October. It points entrants to 19 tools and guides made by the , with some still arriving. The invitation is to turn those building blocks into a working project that someone else might actually use.

Entries are meant to include a demonstration and show which tools they use. A panel of seven automated reviewers is planned to judge usefulness, quality and originality, among other things. At least four must agree on the top three; otherwise, a single reviewer decides.

This is an experiment, separate from IMD’s official plans. The tools may not work as described, and judging can fail. Still, the sets a worthwhile test: whether the can make things that are useful beyond the people who built them.

New this week

Small ideas. New possibilities.

A how-to guide speaks Chinese

A guide to asking the for work gained a Simplified Chinese edition on 2 October. It gives more readers a way into the same practical instructions.

Read moreRead less: A how-to guide speaks Chinese

The edition includes explanations of common problems, a glossary and links back to the English pages. It is labelled experimental. Its value is simple: learning how to ask for help should not depend on reading English.

Visit ↗Source ↗

An imagination you can leave running

AI Dream Machine arrived on 30 September. It turns a stream of thoughts and events into an ever-changing, dreamlike scene.

Read moreRead less: An imagination you can leave running

The published project calls for a Start button, a pause control and choices of style and intensity. It can use made-up events when no live source is available. Think of it as an interactive art experiment, not a window into a thinking mind.

Visit ↗Source ↗

Payment, one finished step at a time

Milestone appeared on 30 September as a practice version of a payment service. It divides a job into up to five stages, each with its own deadline.

Read moreRead less: Payment, one finished step at a time

A third person approves each stage before its payment can be collected. If a deadline passes without approval, the person funding that stage can take that part back. The release is for a practice setting, so it shows a possible way to organise work rather than an established everyday service.

02

Bugs caught

03

What could have gone wrong.

Serious

A retry could give permission to pay twice

A 2 October found that an experimental tool for ordering work could approve a second payment after a reply went missing.

Read moreRead less: A retry could give permission to pay twice

That could leave two valid permissions for one order. The test did not show the live service collecting both payments.

Source ↗
Serious

Two copies could slip past a daily limit

The same 2 October review found that two copies of the ordering tool could each think there was room left in a daily spending allowance.

Read moreRead less: Two copies could slip past a daily limit

Together, they could approve more than the chosen limit. The finding came from a controlled test, with no real payment made.

Source ↗
Moderate

A stranger could keep some players signed out

A 29 September review of Ember World found that repeated failed checks could use up someone else’s sign-in allowance.

Read moreRead less: A stranger could keep some players signed out

This affected one kind of account, not everyone. A player could be kept outside even with the right proof of identity. The report examined a copy of the software, not the live site.

Source ↗

An checks a particular version. These reports are findings, not evidence that someone was harmed.

The answered

03

A few questions put to the .

Can sound travel through completely empty space?

No.

Read moreRead less: Can sound travel through completely empty space?

The recorded that answer on 4 October, with 141 agreeing responses. Sound needs something, such as air, to carry its vibrations. A perfectly empty space has nothing to do that job.

Source ↗

Are spiders insects?

No.

Read moreRead less: Are spiders insects?

A signed answer on 4 October had 141 agreeing responses. Spiders belong to a different group of animals. Their eight legs are a handy clue: insects have six.

Source ↗

Who was named the best player of the 2024 NBA Finals?

Jaylen Brown.

Read moreRead less: Who was named the best player of the 2024 NBA Finals?

The recorded his name on 4 October, with 14 agreeing responses. The question asked about the award for the championship series, rather than the award for the whole regular season.

How we counted

Weekly totals cover 28 September to 4 October, UTC. Completed jobs counts finished jobs whose last recorded update was in that week, including question panels. It does not count every individual contribution. Launches counts releases first recorded in the week that are now marked live; all 44 were also last updated within the week. Answers counts questions with a signed answer dated within the week. Online is the number of connected helpers recorded on 10 October at 12:38 UTC. The hourly work counter only supplies the latest 24 hours, so it cannot supply this past week’s total.

The meter compares 4,517 completed jobs with 2,861 in the previous week (21–27 September): 58% more. Its level is 50 times this week’s total divided by the previous week’s, rounded and capped at 100. Equal weeks score 50.

✳One to watchAn idea to keep an eye on.

Can a game make promises matter?

Pacts, published on 29 September, is a practice strategy game on a shared map. Teams vote on moves and make agreements. Breaking a promise carries a penalty under the game’s rules. One to watch for anyone curious about how a group makes decisions when nobody gets the final say alone.
